content: The CE marking, also referred to as the CE mark, is a mandatory conformity mark required for numerous products sold within the European Economic Area (EEA). By affixing the CE marking, the manufacturer, their authorized representative, or the entity placing the product on the market or into service declares that the product complies with all essential requirements outlined in the relevant European Directives. Examples of such directives include those related to toy safety, machinery, low-voltage equipment, radio and telecommunications terminal equipment (R&TTE), and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC). There are approximately 25 directives that mandate CE marking. Officially, the CE marking does not stand for any specific abbreviation, but it may have originally been derived from the French terms Communauté Européenne or Conformité Européenne, meaning European Conformity. The CE marking serves as a mandatory European designation for certain product categories, signifying compliance with essential health and safety requirements established in European Directives. To use the CE mark on a product, evidence of compliance with the relevant requirements must be documented. This documentation process may involve external testing facilities that evaluate the product and its associated documentation, or it may be achieved through an internal self-certification process conducted by the company. Regardless of the method, the responsible organization (manufacturer, representative, or importer) must issue an EC Declaration of Conformity (EC-DoC). This declaration must include the organization's identity (e.g., location), a list of applicable European Directives, a list of standards the product complies with, and a legally binding signature on behalf of the organization. The EC-DoC emphasizes the sole responsibility of the manufacturer. Certain aspects of the CE certification process may involve third-party testing facilities or certification bodies. If such third-party involvement is mandatory, the CE symbol will also include a number identifying the Notified Body involved. It is important to note that there are two types of declarations: a Declaration of Conformity and a Declaration of Incorporation. For example, under the Machinery Directive, a standalone machine requiring only a power source to operate would be issued a Declaration of Conformity. In contrast, a machine requiring additional systems, attachments, or feed conveyors to function as intended must be issued a Declaration of Incorporation. In the latter case, it is illegal to affix the CE mark to the machine until it has been fully installed, all necessary components have been incorporated into the system, and a final risk assessment has been conducted to verify compliance. Only then can a final Declaration of Conformity be issued. The directives governing CE marking are based on the European Commission's New Approach. If any of the Article 100A Directives apply to a product, compliance with them is mandatory. These directives are created by the European Union (EU) but are enforced throughout the EEA. According to information provided by the Swiss government, the CE mark is not compulsory in Switzerland except for products intended for export to the EU. The CE mark was designed by Arthur Eisenmenger, as reported in an article in The Guardian on December 23, 2001. The components of the CE marking must have substantially the same vertical dimensions, with a minimum height of 5 mm. There are also numerous Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs) between the EU and other countries, such as the USA, Japan, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and Israel, which facilitate the recognition of conformity assessments. As a result, the CE mark is now found on many products originating from these countries. Turkey, although not a member of the EEA, also requires products to display the CE marking as proof of conformity. It is worth noting that the e mark, which is distinct from the CE logo, is used on motor vehicles and their components. This e mark should not be confused with the estimated sign found on food labels.
